## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- Guzik: Moab is the last of the six Gentile nations Amos condemns. Its crime was cruelty to Edom's king, a sin against the dead by dishonouring an Edomite hero's remains. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/
- Ellicott: we don't know what event this refers to. Moab may have desecrated royal tombs or sacrificed the Edomite heir; there's no way to tell. He points to 2 Kings 3:26–27. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Pulpit: the historical books never mention this desecration. He links it to the war in which Edom sided with Israel and Judah against Mesha, king of Moab. He also cites a Jewish tradition, reported by Jerome, that Moab later dug up the Edomite king's bones and dishonoured them in revenge. He rejects the idea that this is the human sacrifice of 2 Kings 3:27. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Calvin: he dislikes the rabbis' story that the ashes were used as lime for plaster, and also an allegorical reading where "bones" means Edom's strength. His view is simply that the king's body was burned, an act of savage inhumanity. Gill, on the same page, does report the plaster tradition, citing the Targum and the Jewish commentators Rashi and Kimchi. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-1.html
- Constable: a peaceful burial was everyone's hope in the ancient Near East, so burning the bones showed contempt for human life made in God's image. Same page.

**v. 2:**
- Ellicott: Kerioth means "towns" but here names one large Moabite town (compare Jeremiah 48:24). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Pulpit: Kerioth is a proper name, possibly a double city. The "tumult" is the noise of war, and Moab is spoken of as a person who dies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm

**v. 3:**
- Pulpit: "judge" (shophet) is probably another word for king, the chief ruler. Moab was later conquered by the Babylonians and faded into insignificance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Matthew Henry: the judge who sentenced the bones to be burned will himself be judged by a higher Judge. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-1.html

**v. 4:**
- Guzik: it is striking that God's own people are judged with the same formula as the pagans. Judah's guilt is greater because they had God's law. When people reject truth, they end up holding on to lies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/
- Pulpit: the nations were condemned for sins against conscience; Judah is condemned for sinning against the written Law. "Lies" means idols, which are nothing and deceive those who trust them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Ellicott: "lies" means false gods. He quotes Pusey's point that children treat their fathers' errors as sacred. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Barnes: whoever doesn't keep God's law in effect despises it, and is then fooled by the lie they chose. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-4.html
- Matthew Henry: an image teaches lies, and one error drags a thousand more after it. Same page.

**v. 5:**
- Pulpit: a brief prophecy of Babylon destroying Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Ellicott: privilege doesn't exempt Judah from punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Guzik: the fire was literal. He applies it to God's purifying fire in believers (1 Corinthians 3; 1 Peter 1 and 4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/

**v. 6:**
- Guzik: this is the rich cruelly exploiting the poor, and God sees it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/
- Scholars disagree here about what kind of "selling" this is; see Part 2.

**v. 7:**
- Ellicott: the oppressors long to see the poor so crushed that they throw dust on their heads in grief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Barnes: the creditors begrudged the poor man even the mourner's dust on his head. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-7.html
- Pulpit: the sin of father and son is close to incest (Leviticus 18). Pulpit adds that the Hebrew wording suggests they did it on purpose, bringing shame on God's name (Romans 2:24). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm

**v. 8:**
- Pulpit: the poor man's outer cloak was his blanket at night, and the law said a pledged cloak must be returned by sunset (Exodus 22:26). These lenders lounged on such cloaks at feasts at the altars of Dan and Bethel. Their wine was bought with fines squeezed out of the poor, and "their god" is the true God worshipped there through a calf image. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Ellicott: he translates "wine of the condemned" as wine of those who were fined. He quotes Pusey on cruelty to the poor being made up for with "a little church-going." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Guzik: he cites Exodus 22:26–27 and pictures one man stacking up immorality, extortion and dishonest gain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/
- Gaebelein: fines paid by condemned people bought wine for heathen orgies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/amos-2.html

**v. 9:**
- Pulpit: the repeated "I" sets God's faithfulness against Israel's ingratitude. The giant-sized description of the Amorite echoes the spies' report in Numbers 13, and "fruit… roots" means "root and branch." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Ellicott: "Amorite" sometimes stood for all the land's inhabitants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Guzik: our walk with God should be driven by gratitude. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/

**v. 10:**
- Pulpit: the Exodus comes last in the list as the high point of God's favour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Ellicott: the forty years were a punishment, but God used them to train wanderers into a nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm

**v. 11:**
- Pulpit: these are two spiritual gifts. Prophets brought God's teaching and Nazirites showed holy living; both were works of God's grace. Pulpit lists Israel's prophets. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Ellicott: quoting W. R. Smith, the Nazirite vow was a protest against Canaanite culture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Guzik: he explains the vow from Numbers 6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/

**v. 12:**
- Wesley: they pressed the Nazirites to drink so that they would break their vow. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-12.html
- Matthew Henry (same page): some Nazirites were coaxed into it and others were shamed into it.
- Pulpit: Israel tried to silence the voices that rebuked it, as was done to Amos himself (7:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm

**v. 13:** The translation is disputed; see Part 2.

**v. 14:**
- Ellicott: this points to invasion and military defeat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Pulpit: "deliver himself" comes three times, like a solemn refrain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Guzik: without God, the strong are not strong enough. He cites 1 Corinthians 10:12 and says we can be weakest where we think we're strong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/

**v. 15:**
- Pulpit: even the skilled archer won't hold his ground. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm

**v. 16:**
- Pulpit: "naked" means throwing off heavy clothes and weapons to run (compare Mark 14:52). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm

## 2. Where commentators differ

In the pages I read, these disagreements were between individual commentators, not between denominations.

**v. 1: Does God care about wrongs done to non-Israelites?**
- Pulpit notes that the Catholic commentators Tirinus and Cornelius a Lapide (the Catholic label is mine, not Pulpit's) saw God punishing wrongs even against heathen nations. Pulpit itself disagrees: Amos condemns only crimes linked to Israel or Judah, so this outrage was meant to shame Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Matthew Henry says the reverse: the victim here was a heathen, not one of God's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-1.html

**v. 4: What are the "lies"?**
- Calvin: "lies" means worship people invent for themselves and defend by their good intentions. Departing from God's word leads to endless delusion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-4.html
- Gill: either idols, or false prophets teaching people to seek life by their own works. Same page.
- Most of the rest (Pulpit, Ellicott, Clarke, Barnes) read it simply as idols.

**v. 6: Bribed judges or debt-slavery?**
- Clarke (Methodist) says corrupt judges took bribes to condemn the innocent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-6.html
- Pulpit's main view is bribery too, though it mentions Pusey's view that debtors were literally sold. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- Barnes and Coffman say it means actual buying and selling of debtors, comparing Amos 8:6. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-6.html
- Ellicott says Amos 8:6 proves the Jewish interpreters and Keil wrong. The sin was twisting the debt-slavery law so a righteous man was enslaved over a debt worth a pair of sandals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm

**v. 7: Temple prostitute or plain immorality?**
- Ellicott: the girl is a cult prostitute in the worship of the goddess Asherah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
- Guzik: probably a ritual prostitute, quoting Clarke. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/
- Coffman: almost certainly idol worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-7.html
- Pulpit thinks the temple-prostitute idea is unnecessary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm

**v. 13: Is God burdened, or is God crushing?**
- Burdened:
  - Guzik takes it as God weighed down by Israel's sin. He quotes Spurgeon that this is a figure of speech, since nothing a person does can actually disturb God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-2/
  - Matthew Henry: God complains of sin as a burden. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-12.html
- Crushing or hemming in:
  - Pulpit prefers Keil's reading, God pressing Israel down with the full force of war. It says the Hebrew verb form tells against the "burdened" reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
  - Ellicott also rejects "burdened," since in context Israel is the victim. His version is "I am pressing down beneath you," like a loaded wagon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/2.htm
  - Clarke: like a cart's wheel grinding the ground. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-13.html
  - Calvin: shutting them into a tight place they can't escape. Same page.
  - Gill gives both readings, plus the Targum's "distress" reading. Same page.

**v. 12, a Methodist application:**
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary uses the Nazirites' abstinence to argue for sobriety today. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/amos/2-12.html

---

## 3. Other views

- **Ancient translations:** Pulpit sets out the old Greek (Septuagint) and Latin (Vulgate) wording at several points. The Vulgate turns "lies" into "idols" (v. 4), and the Septuagint reads v. 8 as curtains hung by the altar to hide immoral acts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm
- **Monks:** Pulpit calls the Nazirites the Old Testament equivalent of Christian monks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/2.htm

**Not covered.** My tools ran out before I could reach these, so nothing from them is included:
- Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org)
- Modern scholarship (netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org)
- Lutheran and Pentecostal sites (lcms.org, 1517.org, ag.org, pneumareview.com, samstorms.org)
- Precept Austin
- Gill's full commentary
- Wesley's notes on wesley.nnu.edu (only short Wesley excerpts quoted on StudyLight)
- Any prosperity or hyper-grace teaching
